title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 234
paragraphs: and the Nile, when it is in flood, goes over not only the Delta but also over the land called Libyan and over the land called Arabian, sometimes as much as two days' journey on each side, at times even more than this, at times less.

As regards the nature of the river, neither from the priests nor from any other man was I able to obtain any knowledge, though I was especially desirous to learn from them about these matters — namely why the Nile comes down increasing in volume from the summer solstice onwards for a hundred days, and then, when it has reached the number of these days, turns and ebbs, failing in its stream, so that through the whole winter season it continues to be low, and remains so until the summer solstice returns. None of these things was I able to learn from the Egyptians when I inquired of them what peculiar property the Nile has, whereby its nature is the opposite of other rivers'. And I made these inquiries desiring to know both this which I say and also why, unlike all other rivers, it does not give rise to any breezes blowing from it.
